title: Genesis 42:18–38

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about money in the sacks, conscience, and Jacob refusing Benjamin.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: We are very guilty concerning our brother—We do not read that they said this during their three days imprisonment; but now when the matter was come to some issue, and they saw themselves still embarrassed, they began to relent. Perhaps Joseph's mention of the fear of God, put them upon consideration, and extorted this reflexion.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 42:21)

reformed.quote: This is a remarkable passage, showing that the sons of Jacob, when reduced to the greatest straits, recall to memory a fratricide committed thirteen years previously. Before affliction pressed upon them, they were in a state of torpor. Moses relates that, even lately, they had spoken without agitation of Joseph's death, as if conscious to themselves of no evil.

context: On the third day Joseph, confessing fear of God, keeps Simeon and sends the rest with grain—and their money. Conscience breaks open on the road and at home; Jacob refuses to send Benjamin, seeing only bereavement, not yet the God who is gathering his sons.

verses.text: Joseph said to them the third day, “Do this, and live, for I fear God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Do this, and live—and the ground: I fear God. Egyptian power names Yahweh’s fear. Life is offered with a condition of honesty, not a vendetta speech.

The fear of God can restrain a wronged man from mere revenge. Joseph’s agency is holy here: he chooses life for them under God’s eye.
verses.reformedNotes:
Third-day word: live, because I fear God. The governor locates his policy in piety.

The fear of God in Joseph is the fear God Himself planted through pit, prison, and throne. Mercy to the brothers flows from that fear.

verses.text: If you are honest men, then let one of your brothers be bound in your prison; but you go, carry grain for the famine of your houses.
verses.arminianNotes:
The terms ease: one confined, the rest carry grain home. Households will not starve while the test runs.

Honesty is still the if. Grace feeds even the guilty family; it also requires a brother left behind as pledge. They must choose whom to leave.
verses.reformedNotes:
Grain for famine of your households: provision inside the proving.

God will not let Jacob’s house die while He heals it. Custody of one and bread for many is severe kindness.

verses.text: Bring your youngest brother to me; so will your words be verified, and you won’t die.” They did so.
verses.arminianNotes:
Bring Benjamin, words verified, you shall not die. They did so—consent to the terms.

Classical Arminians: they act. Verification is a moral path they can walk or later refuse at home (v. 38). Enabling care (grain) does not erase the demand for truth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Youngest brother as the verifier. They comply in Egypt.

“You won’t die” is Joseph’s mouth and God’s intent. The family of promise is being kept through a hard obedience.

verses.text: They said to one another, “We are certainly guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn’t listen. Therefore this distress has come upon us.”
verses.arminianNotes:
At last: in truth we are guilty. They remember Joseph’s begging and their closed ears. Present distress is read as echo, not chance.

Arminian heart of the chapter: conscience still speaks years later. Grace that they did not listen to in the pit now corners them toward confession. Guilt is true and theirs; repentance remains a responsible turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Guilty concerning our brother: the Spirit of truth uses famine and roughness to surface the pit.

God is not mocked, and God is not finished. The distress He appoints becomes the lantern on their old sin, that mercy may follow.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat this as true guilt, not superstition. Arminians typically stress a resistible, long-ignored conscience now answering; Reformed interpreters stress God’s appointed distress that makes the buried sin speak.

verses.text: Reuben answered them, saying, “Didn’t I tell you, saying, ‘Don’t sin against the child,’ and you wouldn’t listen? Therefore also, behold, his blood is required.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Reuben recalls his protest (37:21–22) and names a reckoning for blood. Being right then does not heal the family now.

Pastorally: “I told you so” can be accurate and still thin. Each brother remains accountable. Grace calls for shared repentance, not scorekeeping only.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reckoning for his blood: Reuben hears justice arriving.

Blood has a voice (4:10). God can reckon without Joseph being dead—and without the brothers yet knowing he lives.

verses.text: They didn’t know that Joseph understood them; for there was an interpreter between them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The interpreter is a wall. They confess in Hebrew, thinking the lord does not hear.

Hidden audience does not make the words less true. Grace sometimes lets us speak honesty before we know who is listening.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joseph understands; they do not know. Knowledge still runs one way.

The brother they silenced now hears the confession in their own tongue.

verses.text: He turned himself away from them, and wept. Then he returned to them, and spoke to them, and took Simeon from among them, and bound him before their eyes.
verses.arminianNotes:
He weeps, then binds Simeon before their eyes. Tears and firmness together—not ice, not collapse.

Holy emotion and holy limit can share a minute. Joseph chooses mercy’s pace. Binding Simeon is still a hard act they must watch; weeping shows the heart underneath.
verses.reformedNotes:
Weeping hidden, Simeon bound in public. Love and test in one man.

God has kept a tender heart on the throne of Egypt. The binding is not the last gesture; the tears tell the end of the story in advance.

verses.text: Then Joseph gave a command to fill their bags with grain, and to restore each man’s money into his sack, and to give them food for the way. So it was done to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Grain, money returned, provisions—gift under the guise of sale. Kindness they cannot yet interpret.

The brothers receive provision they did not earn. Grace often precedes full confession. They will tremble at the money; the gift is still gift.
verses.reformedNotes:
Orders given: fill, replace, provision. Done for them—passive of a mercy they did not request.

The governor’s generosity is God’s way of keeping Jacob alive and unsettling the brothers toward Himself (v. 28).

verses.text: They loaded their donkeys with their grain, and departed from there.
verses.arminianNotes:
They load and leave—Simeon behind, grain on the animals. The road home begins under mixed cargo: food and fear.

Pastorally: going home with bread is not yet going home reconciled. The next lodging will test how they read God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The brothers depart with their grain. The mission Jacob named is outwardly success.

They leave by Joseph’s permission and God’s timing. Simeon in custody is the thread that will pull Benjamin south.

verses.text: As one of them opened his sack to give his donkey food in the lodging place, he saw his money. Behold, it was in the mouth of his sack.
verses.arminianNotes:
At the lodging, fodder first—then money. Behold, it was in the mouth of the sack. An ordinary stop becomes a shock.

God can meet people on the way, not only at altars. What they do with the discovery will show whether fear becomes faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
One sack, one lodging, silver visible. Providence arranges a small apocalypse on the road.

Nothing in the mouth of the sack is luck. The returned price is a sign they will name as God’s doing.

verses.text: He said to his brothers, “My money is restored! Behold, it is in my sack!” Their hearts failed them, and they turned trembling to one another, saying, “What is this that God has done to us?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Hearts fail; they tremble: What is this that God has done to us? They finally say God, not only “the man.”

Classical Arminians: this is awakening, still mixed with dread. Grace convicts; they may yet flee or seek mercy. Naming God as actor is the beginning of wisdom if it leads to repentance, not only panic.
verses.reformedNotes:
Money put back becomes theology: God has done this.

They are right. God is the deep cause. The trembling is not yet trust, but it is truer than “honest men” in v. 11.
verses.keyContrast: Both welcome the God-question. Arminians stress a sincere, accountable waking of conscience that must still choose repentance; Reformed interpreters emphasize God’s own act in the sack as the cause of their fear.

verses.text: They came to Jacob their father, to the land of Canaan, and told him all that had happened to them, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Home, and they tell Jacob all that happened—selecting, as speakers do. The father must now enter the test.

Testimony to a parent is a duty. Completeness will be tested by what they do with Benjamin next.
verses.reformedNotes:
Canaan hears Egypt’s story through sons’ mouths.

The household of promise is being briefed by providence, even when the briefing is partial and afraid.

verses.text: “The man, the lord of the land, spoke roughly with us, and took us for spies of the country.
verses.arminianNotes:
They lead with the man’s roughness and the spy charge. Joseph remains “the man.”

They report the wound, not yet the brother. Grace can work with incomplete stories on the way to a fuller one.
verses.reformedNotes:
Lord of the land, rough speech, spies: the public facts.

They cannot name the lord as Joseph. God still writes the story they misfile as foreign threat.

verses.text: We said to him, ‘We are honest men. We are no spies.
verses.arminianNotes:
They repeat the honest-men line to Jacob. The claim has already cracked on the road (v. 21).

Rehearsing innocence to a father is tempting. Better to bring him the guilt they confessed to each other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Honest men, never spies—replayed at home.

The gap between this report and v. 21 is itself revelatory. God has begun a work their summary has not caught up with.

verses.text: We are twelve brothers, sons of our father; one is no more, and the youngest is today with our father in the land of Canaan.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Twelve, one no more, youngest here. They still speak Joseph’s absence as fate.

In practice: family math without confession keeps the wound closed. Grace invites Jacob’s house to a truer count.
verses.reformedNotes:
The same formula spoken in Egypt is now Canaan’s news.

“One is no more” is false in fact, true in their guilt. God is about to correct the census.

verses.text: The man, the lord of the land, said to us, ‘By this I will know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain for the famine of your houses, and go your way.
verses.arminianNotes:
They transmit the test: leave one, take grain, go. Simeon’s absence is explained as the lord’s proof.

The terms are now Jacob’s burden too. Households have bread; a son is collateral. Responsible love must face both.
verses.reformedNotes:
Honest men proven by a brother left and grain carried.

God has placed a pledge in Egypt so this family cannot settle back into the old silence.

verses.text: Bring your youngest brother to me. Then I will know that you are not spies, but that you are honest men. So I will deliver your brother to you, and you shall trade in the land.’”
verses.arminianNotes:
Benjamin for Simeon and for trade in the land. The future of the family is tied to the youngest going down.

Honesty will cost Jacob his fear. Grace does not mock the cost; it still asks the step.
verses.reformedNotes:
Youngest brother as the key to delivery and trade.

God is opening Egypt as refuge (later Goshen) through this hard condition. Promise and testing are woven together here.

verses.text: As they emptied their sacks, behold, each man’s bundle of money was in his sack. When they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid.
verses.arminianNotes:
Every sack, every bundle—father and sons afraid together. What looked like theft-trap lands in Jacob’s tent.

Shared fear can become shared prayer. It can also become shared refusal (v. 38). The money is a fork.
verses.reformedNotes:
All the silver visible at once. Fear fills the household of Israel.

God makes the sign unmistakable. Fear of God (v. 28) now includes the patriarch, who still misreads the Giver.

verses.text: Jacob, their father, said to them, “You have bereaved me of my children! Joseph is no more, Simeon is no more, and you want to take Benjamin away. All these things are against me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Bereaved… all these things are against me. Jacob totals losses and feels only opposition. He does not yet say God is for him.

Faith can speak this way and be wrong. Grace still invites a larger reading. The sons’ old lie about Joseph feeds this despair; they remain responsible for that grief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joseph no more, Simeon no more, Benjamin next: Jacob’s ledger of against-me.

The reader knows the ledger is false. All this has come, through their sin and God’s rule, for life (50:20). The patriarch’s lament is not the narrator’s last word.

verses.text: Reuben spoke to his father, saying, “Kill my two sons, if I don’t bring him to you. Entrust him to my care, and I will bring him to you again.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Reuben offers his two sons as surety—a rash pledge. Zeal to fix the past overreaches.

Desperate guarantees are not the same as trustworthy care. Grace prefers truth and patience to bargaining in grandchildren’s blood.
verses.reformedNotes:
Kill my two sons: Reuben’s mouth outruns wisdom. Reuben’s intensity as firstborn offers little real help.

Human surety cannot calm Jacob. Only God’s keeping of Benjamin will suffice, and Reuben is not that keeper.

verses.text: He said, “My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he only is left. If harm happens to him along the way in which you go, then you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol.”
verses.arminianNotes:
My son shall not go down. Benjamin is the only one left in Jacob’s Rachel-heart. The chapter ends on refusal and Sheol-fear.

Jacob refuses. Jacob is not forced here. Grace will have to meet him again (ch. 43) so that love of the living son does not starve the household. Responsible fatherhood must yet trust God with Benjamin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Gray hairs to Sheol: Jacob chooses preservation of Benjamin over Simeon’s return and over the lord’s terms.

Reformed hope under the no: the God who already holds Joseph will not let this refusal be final. Famine and promise will press until the son goes down—and the family lives.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse to mock Jacob’s grief. Arminians stress his accountable, fearful refusal that must still yield; Reformed interpreters stress that God’s purpose to save this house will outlast the patriarch’s no.
